body: Phone face down beside the chemistry book: a rule the girl keeps for about nine minutes at a stretch. Twenty past four, and she is at the dining table with the book open. Her grandmother is in the chair by the window with the volume too loud on a programme she has seen before. Without looking away from the screen she asks, in Spanish, whether the girl wants the rest of the rice. The girl says in a bit, in English, without looking up. The grandmother says something else, in Spanish, about a cousin and a car. The girl says that is so annoying, in English. Neither notices that anything has occurred.

That arrangement is so ordinary in immigrant houses that it barely gets remarked on, and it works. For years it works. Everybody understands everybody, nothing is repeated, and the household runs on it the way it runs on the boiler.
It works until it is asked to carry weight. The parents are most themselves in one language and the children in another, and nobody chose this.

The places it strains are always the same four, and they are worth naming, because it is not the ordinary conversation that fails. It is comfort, correction, apology and prayer. Those are the registers a person only ever has in the language they were formed in — the language they were held in as a small child, told off in, and first heard someone pray over them in. A person can acquire vocabulary and grammar and even humour in a second language, and go decades sounding fluent, and still have nothing there when the moment requires them to say something that costs. The words are available. The register is not.

The band carries 40 international stations across 29 languages, one frequency to one language. Familia Inspire holds HM 320.30 in Spanish and is on air. Jubilee Prayers in Spanish holds HM 350.50 — continuous oración and the Salmos — and it is assigned, in build and not yet on air.

The result is that both people in the conversation are misread by the other, and both are misled by fluency rather than by feeling. A parent consoling a grown child in a second language comes out stiffer, flatter and more distant than they are, and sounds like someone who does not much care. A child explaining something painful in the parents’ language comes out younger and less competent than they are, and sounds like someone who has not thought it through. Each hears the other exactly as they did not intend. Neither is aware that anything has been lost in the crossing, because the sentences were all correct.

Nothing in the wider culture is arranged to help with this and a good deal makes it worse. The advice available is about language preservation, which is a school subject, or about family communication, which assumes everybody in the room shares a first language and merely needs to listen better. Meanwhile the services people live inside are personalised to the individual, so every member of the household is served a different set of words. A family that once had the same programme, the same station and the same hymns has been quietly subdivided, and the subdivision is invisible because each part of it is an improvement.

On this dial the international frequencies are hosted in their own languages rather than dubbed into them afterwards, which matters more here than it looks. A dubbed station gives a household the content twice and the register never. A station made by people who pray in that language carries the things that are not in the vocabulary list: where the pauses go, which phrases are used at a funeral, the particular cadence a grandmother would recognise as praying rather than as talking about God.
So what actually helps? Not, unfortunately, anything that sounds like a solution.

The obvious answer is to fix the language, and it deserves a fair hearing because it is not wrong. Send the children to Saturday classes, insist they answer their grandmother properly, spend the money, keep it up for a decade. Families who do this get something real, and their children thank them at thirty. But it does not solve the thing this article is about. Classroom Spanish gives a person a second language they can use. It does not give them the language they were comforted in, because that is not built by instruction — it is built by having been small and frightened while somebody spoke it over you. You cannot retrofit a register.
What is missing is not fluency. It is common property.

Her son is thirty-six and his marriage has ended, and he is at her table on a Tuesday afternoon because he has nowhere else to be at that hour. She makes coffee she does not want in order to have something to do with her hands. Then she says, in careful English, that everything will be fine. It comes out flat as a form letter, he hears a woman with nothing to say to him, and something in him closes for the afternoon. What he does not hear, because it happens in the next room while she is putting the cups away, is that she has been praying under her breath about him since seven that morning, in Spanish, in the words her own mother used, with his name in the middle of them.
Both of those things are the same woman in the same hour. Only one of them made it across the kitchen.

There is a cost to saying this plainly, and it is that no radio station is going to fix it. A frequency cannot give a father the register he does not have. It will not repair the conversation that went wrong on Tuesday, and any article implying otherwise is selling something. The households where this hurts most are usually the ones with the least room in the week to do anything about it, and a suggestion that they add a listening habit to their obligations is not much of a gift.

But shared material is not an obligation, which is the whole reason it works. It costs a household nothing to have the same thing audible in the same room, and it accumulates without anybody attending to it. A song both generations know, a prayer said the same way every time, a phrase that has been in the house often enough to belong to everybody — these are not solutions to the problem. They are stock. They are what a person reaches for on the Tuesday when their own words have failed, and the reason they are there to reach for is that nobody was trying to acquire them.

So the modest claim is the true one. A station cannot translate a mother to her son. What it can do is put words in the room that already belong to both of them, so that on the day the conversation strains there is something in the house that does not have to be translated in the moment, because it was common property before anybody needed it. That is a small function. It is also the one thing the household in this article is actually short of.
All of which is theory until something is actually playing. So here is the part that is not theory.

There is more than one way to do this and the honest answer depends on your house. If the older generation is the one that is most alone in the building, HM 320.30 — Familia Inspire (Español) — is the frequency to leave on, and Mañana Familia at eight in the morning is the hour to do it. But there is a second option, and for a house where the children have already gone over to English it is the better one, because it does not ask either generation to cross first.

Start at HM 310.90 — Latin Worship (English-Spanish), hosted by Santiago Inspire, carrying 482 tracks of Latin ballad, cumbia, samba and liturgical worship sung in English, relayed from Miami, Los Angeles and San Antonio. It is the one frequency on this dial that requires no translation in either direction at once. The music is the inheritance the grandmother grew up inside and will recognise from the first bar without being told what it is. The words are the language the girl at the dining table thinks in. Neither of them has to be a guest, and neither has to perform a competence they do not have, which is the exact condition under which shared material actually accumulates.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card — open kJubilee.com on whatever phone or laptop is nearest, press play, and it plays. It is deliberately built for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have. If you want it closer to hand, add the page to your home screen and it will open like anything else on it. And do make yourself an account while you are there. It keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how this band learns which frequencies people are genuinely reaching for, which is how the next one gets built.

So take this as an invitation rather than an offer, and take it in the least ambitious way available. Put HM 310.90 on in the room where everybody passes through, at the hour when everybody does, and then say nothing about it at all. Do not explain it, do not ask anybody whether they like it, and do not expect the Tuesday conversation to go differently next month. Leave it running for a season and let the house accumulate a few things nobody in it had to choose. That is how a household comes by anything it holds in common, and it has never once happened on purpose.
